name: Sankaranarayanar Temple, Sankarankovil
deity: Sankaranarayanar, the united form of Shiva and Vishnu (Hari-Hara), with Sankara Linga Swami and the goddess Gomathi Amman
period: Pandya foundation traditionally of the 10th century, with later Nayak additions
summary: Sankaranarayanar is the Hari-Hara temple of Sankarankovil, where Shiva and Vishnu are worshipped as one form and where, tradition says, Gomathi Amman's penance brought the Lord to her in that united shape.

sections.history: Sankarankovil, in the Tenkasi country of the deep south, takes its name from the temple. Local tradition credits it to the Pandya king Ukkira Pandiyan and places the foundation around the tenth century; later patrons, including the Nayaks, enlarged it and raised its nine-tiered rajagopuram. It is a rare shrine devoted to the oneness of Shiva and Vishnu, drawing Shaiva and Vaishnava devotees alike, and it stands among the principal temples of the Tirunelveli region, a place where two great streams of devotion meet in a single sanctum.
sections.architecture: The nine-tier rajagopuram rises over the entrance, and the complex holds three principal sanctums: those of Sankara Linga Swami, the Shiva form, of Gomathi Amman, and of Sankaranarayanar. Before the Amman shrine is a Sri Chakra peetham. A sacred tank, the Nagasunai, is said to have been dug by the two serpent kings of the legend. Dravidian corridors and pillared halls surround the shrines, in the long, unhurried manner of the southern temples.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that two serpent kings, Sankan, a devotee of Shiva, and Padman, a devotee of Vishnu, quarrelled over which god was greater. Gomathi, the goddess here, undertook penance in the punnai forest, asking to see the Lord in a form that joins both. Shiva appeared as Sankaranarayanar, half Shiva and half Vishnu, on the Uthiradam star in the month of Adi, and the dispute ended. The tale teaches that the two are one.
sections.festivals: The Aadi Thapasu festival, in July or August, commemorates Gomathi's penance and the appearance of the Lord as Sankaranarayanar, and is the temple's greatest celebration, drawing devotees from across the region. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham and the festivals of both Shiva and Vishnu are kept through the year. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Enter beneath the rajagopuram and go first to the sanctum of Sankaranarayanar, where a single image honours Shiva and Vishnu together. Devotees receive a pinch of sacred ant-hill earth as prasad, and many sit in prayer before the Sri Chakra in Gomathi Amman's shrine. Walk the corridors and the Nagasunai tank at an easy pace. The town is lively on festival days and quiet on others, and the temple rewards those who come in the cool of the morning.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Sankarankovil lies in Tenkasi district, roughly 50 km from Tirunelveli, and is served by buses from Tirunelveli, Madurai, Tenkasi and Rajapalayam. Tirunelveli Junction is the nearest major railhead. Thoothukudi Airport and Madurai Airport are the nearest airports, roughly 90 km and 140 km away. The temple stands in the centre of the town, and autos are easily found.
